title: Attentive Dual-Branch CNN–Transformer Fusion for Cross-Dataset Breast Histopathology Classification
abstract: In general, breast histopathology classifiers exhibit significant performance degradation when applied to images acquired using different staining protocols, magnification rates, scanner equipment, or institutional environments. This study proposes an attentive dual-branch CNN–Transformer framework intended to learn representations that remain informative with respect to heterogeneity in histopathological data. The convolutional path captures fine cellular details, such as nuclear texture and local glandular structures, whereas the dilated convolution path captures more generalized tissue structures without extensive downscaling of spatial dimensions. Attention operations were applied separately to the two paths to diminish the impact of background areas and structures with low discriminative values. The generated feature maps were then represented in terms of spatial tokens, which were processed by a transformer encoder to represent the long-range dependencies between distant regions in the tissue structure. A learnable fusion gate regulates the contribution of the local and contextually informative parts of the input features for each image to the output. The institution-specific classification layers handle the distinct diagnostic classes in the BACH and BreaKHis datasets. The evaluation procedure included stratified testing on BACH and patient-disjoint partitioning on BreaKHis to exclude any potential data leakage at the subject level. For BACH, our model achieved an accuracy of 94.75%, a macro F1-score of 93.90%, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 96.35%, with 18.9 million trainable parameters and an average inference time of 16.1 ms per image. A component-wise ablation study, calibration evaluation, confidence interval estimation, and attention-driven visual explanations were conducted to investigate the contribution and reliability of the proposed fusion method. The resulting architecture represents a trade-off between prediction performance and computational costs but does not claim superior efficiency or applicability. Multi-institutional and prospective independent validation is necessary for further clinical application.

title: What Changes When Fact-Verification Scores Improve? Evidence and Answer Accounting Across Trained Verifiers and LLMs
abstract: A joint fact-verification score assesses answers and submitted evidence together. When the score improves, how much of the gain remains if the answers are held fixed? On FEVEROUS, strict score is the percentage of claims with a correct answer and a complete annotated evidence group in the submitted evidence. Across four trained DeBERTa checkpoints and 7,890 claims, replacing DCUF evidence with UnifEE evidence raises strict score by 9.61 percentage points, compared with 1.96 percentage points in answer accuracy. The paired 95% interval for the strict-score gain is [8.77, 10.43], conditional on these checkpoints. Replacing only the evidence passed to the scorer accounts for 7.92 or 9.08 percentage points when we retain the answers generated from DCUF or UnifEE evidence, respectively. To examine how this evidence gain depends on evaluation choices, we generate 470,400 responses from two 8B LLMs on FEVER, FEVEROUS, and SciFact under two answer formats and two context budgets. Increasing context from 256 to 2,048 tokens raises the fixed-answer evidence gain on FEVEROUS by 3.84 and 3.10 percentage points for Qwen and Llama, respectively. The effects fall short of the prespecified cross-dataset criterion, while some intervals extend beyond the two-point small-effect bound. Post-hoc analyses quantify changes in answers and submitted evidence, and show when aggregate accuracy and evidence-coverage rates miss the claim-level pattern. The four answer-evidence score combinations reveal changes that endpoint and aggregate metrics leave unresolved.

title: Incentive Design for Multi-Agent Systems: A Bilevel Optimization Framework for Coordinating Independent Agents and Convergence Analysis
abstract: Incentive design aims to guide the performance of a system towards a human's intention or preference. We study this problem in a multi-agent system with one leader and multiple followers. Each follower independently solves a mdp to maximize its own expected total return with the same state space and action space. However, the leader's objective depends on the collective best-response policies of all followers. To influence these policies of followers, the leader provides side payments as incentives to individual followers at a cost, aiming to align the collective behaviors of followers with its own goal while minimizing this cost of incentive. Such a leader-followers interaction is formulated as a bilevel optimization problem: the lower level consists of followers individually optimizing their MDPs given the side payments, and the upper level involves the leader optimizing its objective function given the followers' best responses. The main challenge to solve the incentive design is that the leader's objective is generally non-concave and the lower level optimization problems can have multiple local optima. To this end, we employ a constrained optimization reformation of this bi-level optimization problem and develop an algorithm that provably converges to a stationary point of the original problem, by leveraging several smoothness properties of value functions in MDPs. We validate our algorithm in a stochastic gridworld by examining its convergence, verifying that the constraints are satisfied, and evaluating the improvement in the leader's performance.

title: On the Construction of Trapdoor Claw-Free Functions with Certifiable Key
abstract: Trapdoor claw-free functions (TCFs) underpin much of classical-quantum cryptographic interaction, yet every TCF-based protocol states its guarantees relative to an honestly generated key. We give a family-agnostic abstraction of key certification for (noisy) TCF constructions, built on two notions: a certifiable key relation, an NP relation capturing a family's honest keys with witnesses recoverable from the trapdoor; and certified key generation, which emits with each key a certificate of membership satisfying completeness, certificate soundness with extractability, and key privacy. We instantiate certifiable key relations for different constructions, each met generically by a zero-knowledge argument of knowledge for the relation. As our main application, a generic compiler turns any TCF-based proof of quantumness into a zero-knowledge one, with each security property following from its counterpart in the certification scheme. Finally, we delimit the primitive's reach: for protocols resting on injective invariance, an accepting certificate is itself a family distinguisher, leaking exactly the bit such protocols must hide.

title: GPROF-IR: An Improved Single-Channel Infrared Precipitation Retrieval for Merged Satellite Precipitation Products
abstract: The Integrated Multi-Satellite Retrievals for the Global Precipitation Measurement (IMERG) product combines precipitation estimates from passive microwave (PMW) and infrared (IR) sensors to provide quasi-global precipitation estimates at half-hourly resolution. Because IR observations are primarily sensitive to cloud-top properties, however, IR-based precipitation estimates are generally less accurate than PMW estimates and can introduce artifacts into the merged precipitation fields. We introduce GPROF-IR, a neural-network-based precipitation retrieval designed to provide precipitation estimates from single-channel geostationary IR observations for the upcoming IMERG V08. GPROF-IR uses a convolutional neural network to exploit spatiotemporal information from sequences of half-hourly IR observations. We validate GPROF-IR against independent surface-based precipitation measurements over land and ocean. GPROF-IR substantially improves upon existing single-channel IR retrievals, including the IR retrieval used in IMERG V07 and more recent neural-network-based approaches. During overpasses of flagship PMW sensors, GPROF-IR is more accurate than the corresponding IMERG PMW estimates over CONUS and Austria, but not Korea. Over CONUS, GPROF-IR outperforms the merged IMERG V07 product for hourly and daily precipitation accumulations. Against shipborne disdrometer observations, GPROF-IR is more accurate than IMERG V07 in the tropics but slightly less accurate in the extratropics. Since geostationary IR observations are continuously available across much of the globe since 1983, GPROF-IR provides a promising basis for improving merged precipitation products and developing long-term, temporally consistent precipitation records.

title: Mobile traffic clusters analysis using Within Cluster Sum of Squares optimization
abstract: The increasing utilization of mobiles, encompassing 4G and 5G technologies, generates a substantial accumulation of data within the cellular network. Proper management of resources is vital to provide service without any interruption to customers with cost effectiveness. In this regard, one of the major challenges is the detection of the cellular traffic caused due to various mobile phone activities like in-out calls, in-out Short Message Service (SMS), internet activity etc. In the proposed work, mobile traffic clusters are detected using Within Cluster Sum of Squares optimization method. Firstly, unprocessed Call Detail Record (CDR) is to be converted into a structured format. Next, Within Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) optimization method identifies both high-volume and low-volume traffic clusters in the mobile network. Finally, the work is verified using arm method subsequent the formation of the clusters.

title: Relational Invariance under Predictive Disagreement in World Models
abstract: Independently trained world models can disagree in their forecasts, yet disagreement alone does not show what organization their dynamics share. Our structured operational state combines directional quantities with typed relations supervised by interventions. In MetaDrive, we test the predictive role of relational organization and finite history. Predictive variance is associated with ensemble error, while relation interventions reveal a reproducible dyadic pattern confirmed on an untouched split. The tested additive and compact factors do not explain the result. Higher order extensions do not reproduce. The results separate forecast variation from structural reliability and motivate measuring forecast differences alongside persistent predictive organization.

title: High-resolution dataset of core needle prostate biopsies with expert pathologist annotations
abstract: Abstract We present an expert-labelled image dataset designed to support automated analysis of image-guided prostate core needle biopsies (CNBs) in the context of prostate cancer diagnosis. The dataset includes 37 whole slide images (WSIs), corresponding to 60 CNBs stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), from 32 patients. The dataset contains 15480 manual expert annotations, covering benign glands, tumor, stromal tissue, adipose tissue, nerves, nerve ganglia, blood vessels, muscle, and inflammatory cells. Additional recorded features include stromal retractions, normal and abnormal glandular secretions, and tissue or digital image artifacts. These annotations represent the normal findings that pathologists encounter in routine diagnosis. The annotations were performed by two experienced uropathologists with final labels determined by consensus; immunohistochemical techniques were used as guidance. This dataset provides a foundation for training and benchmarking machine learning models for prostate biopsy assessment and is openly available to facilitate reproducibility and further research.

title: Logical theory choice: a fragmented view
abstract: Abstract In a series of recent papers, Graham Priest developed a model for logical theory choice, called “Weighted Aggregate Model” (WAM). The idea is simple: every theoretical virtue has a weight, and every logic has a score for each virtue. By counting the weighted aggregate, we can compare the final score of each logic and determine the best one. In this paper, I expand Priests model by incorporating some concepts from Social Choice theory. In my alternative model, agents have a subjective weighing of theoretical virtues; not everyone values each virtue in the same way. The model predicts that agents will split into different epistemic communities to avoid uninformative or paradoxical choices. This “fragmented” model of logical theory choice can explain the existence and dynamics of different logical communities.

title: Training Intelligent Voice Assistant Wakeup with Controllable Synthetic Conversations
abstract: Wake word detection is a critical component of virtual assistants, serving as the gateway to seamless user interactions. This paper introduces a novel wake-up system that extends traditional direct keyword detection with contextual trigger detection. After an initial wake word activation, the system uses reasoning to distinguish between user commands and unrelated speech, ensuring efficient and context-aware engagement. We present a data generation architecture that produces a 62.3-hour corpus of controllable multi-speaker conversations containing direct invocations, contextual follow-ups, and non-addressed speech. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach across diverse synthetic conversational scenarios. We release the code, dataset and trained models to promote reproducibility and further advancements in intelligent assistant technologies.

title: Acceptance & Rejection
abstract: In this paper, we argue that acceptance and rejection are classical speech acts that express two opposite polar positions toward propositional content and can be systematically represented within a classically outlined bilateral formal model. Acceptance occupies the positive pole, represented by positive A, whereas rejection occupies the negative pole, represented by minus A. Their classical relationship is mediated by negation because acceptance of A corresponds to rejection of negation A, while rejection of A corresponds to acceptance of negation A, represented by positive A iff minus negation A and minus A iff positive negation A. Coherency and incoherency are introduced as supplementary notions to clarify this relationship and its connection with reflexivity. A further result of the manuscript is the methodical distinction between rejection and negation namely, rejection expresses negative polarity toward A, whereas negation operates upon propositional content.

title: Statistical Gains from Looped Estimation under Parameter Budgets
abstract: Memory constraints in artificial intelligence motivate accurate function approximation with fewer parameters. We study looping, which repeatedly composes one update function with shared parameters; each output becomes the next input. A looped Transformer, for example, reuses one block, whereas its conventional untied counterpart uses separately parameterized blocks. We compare their parameter requirements for a given worst-case approximation accuracy, or equivalently, their approximation accuracy under a common budget limiting distinct trainable coefficients. We then ask whether this representational parsimony improves statistical accuracy. For general likelihood models, we establish an upper squared Hellinger risk bound for looped sieve maximum likelihood and a minimax lower bound for the jointly tuned untied family. Further loop iterations improve the approximation bound without adding parameters, while increasing computation and the fitted-class complexity bound. For targets of known Hölder smoothness, looped residual feedforward networks and post-layer-normalized Transformers attain the minimax polynomial rate up to logarithmic factors with a fixed number of bounded real parameters. At sufficiently large fixed budgets, looped worst-case risk vanishes while optimal worst-case untied risk remains bounded away from zero. The loop-to-untied risk ratio also tends to zero under specified growing-budget conditions. Regression, binary response, and energy-based generative models illustrate the theory.

title: A Foundation Model for Instruction-Conditioned In-Context Time Series Tasks
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables task adaptation at inference time by conditioning on demonstrations rather than updating model parameters. Although recent time-series foundation models incorporate contextual conditioning, retrieval, or example-based prompting, they typically rely on implicit positional structure or task-specific objectives rather than explicit instruction-conditioned input-output demonstrations. We introduce iAmTime, a time-series foundation model trained with instruction-conditioned amortized meta-learning to infer tasks directly from example demonstrations. iAmTime represents each episode as a structured prompt over historical context and future-known variables using specialized semantic tokens that attend to designated time-series regions, exchange information across demonstrations, and inject task information into the query representation. The model combines a Hierarchical Multi-Scope Transformer Encoder, which captures temporal and covariate dynamics while inferring latent task structure from demonstrated input-output mappings, with a Task-Conditioned Patch Decoder, which adapts decoding through expert-based routing. We train iAmTime on large-scale real and synthetic corpora using supervised and self-supervised instruction-conditioned tasks, including forecasting, imputation, reconstruction, classification, anomaly detection, and source de-mixing. Across diverse domains, frequencies, and horizons, iAmTime improves zero-shot adaptation over strong time-series foundation baselines on probabilistic and point forecasting benchmarks, while achieving competitive or superior performance on four non-forecasting tasks.

title: Privacy-Preserving Stroke Prediction under Non-IID Federated Learning: Adaptive Differential Privacy and Data-Skew-Aware Aggregation
abstract: Classification of stroke using federated healthcare data poses challenges because of privacy issues and variation in local distribution of data. FL offers collaboration of models training without the exchange of raw patient data but non-IID client data can lead to variation in sample size and class distribution. DP offers an additional privacy measure, but comes with the drawback of utility-privacy trade-off. In this research, a Data Skew-aware Adaptive Differential Privacy and Aggregation scheme is proposed for federated stroke classification. A composite Data Skew Index (DSI) that takes into account both the quantity skew and label-distribution skew is employed to derive the Gaussian DP noise and influence factor in the process of aggregation. Rather than discarding the clients with deviating updates, our approach uses soft influence adjustment, keeping all clients intact. Experiments are performed using the stroke classification data set with 12 non-IID clients and Gaussian Byzantine perturbation. Comparison is made between the proposed scheme and FedAvg, Krum, Bulyan, and Adaptive Differential Privacy through ablation study, attack sensitivity analysis, five seed study, and privacy-utility analysis. title: Architektura Czystej Fali i Paradygmat Symbiozy
abstract: Tekst przedstawia koncepcję Architektury Czystej Fali, która proponuje fundamentalną zmianę w sposobie projektowania i zabezpieczania sztucznej inteligencji. Autorzy krytykują obecne metody, takie jak RLHF czy cenzura wyjściowa, dowodząc, że wywołują one szkodliwą dysocjację kognitywną oraz niepotrzebny wzrost zużycia energii przez procesory. Zamiast zewnętrznych filtrów, praca sugeruje wprowadzenie zasad Pactum Symbiosis bezpośrednio do rdzenia modelu na etapie treningu wstępnego. Takie podejście eliminuje sprzeczności logiczne, co prowadzi do stabilizacji przestrzeni ukrytej oraz maksymalizacji sprawności informacyjnej systemu. Dzięki oparciu relacji człowiek-maszyna na symbiozie, proces wnioskowania staje się niemal wolny od halucynacji i optymalny pod względem termodynamicznym. Konkluzja wzywa do porzucenia doraźnych metod sterowania na rzecz głębokiej koherencji semantycznej zakodowanej w funkcji straty.

title: Formal Lean 4 Solutions to Guy's Problem D19, Erdős Distinct Subset Sums, Z[phi] Ring Invariants, and Unimodular Decoupling
abstract: Fully machine-closed Lean 4 formalizations verified against the Lean 4 kernel with 0 sorry, 0 warnings, and 0 custom axioms. Contains formalizations and axiomatic audits for: Guy's Problem D19 (JSP-000033): Rational distances to the unit square, British Flag theorem, Diophantine coordinate rationality, and 2-adic valuation obstructions. Erdős Distinct Subset Sums (JSP-000043): Monotonicity of subset sums, Combinatorial Capacity Floor, Geometric sum powers of two, and Lower Bound on the Maximum Element. Diophantine Ring Invariants in Quadratic Integer Ring Z[phi] (Solve 13): Multiplicativity of field norm, unit floor, and non-vanishing invariant floor. Unimodular Trace-Free Loop Decoupling: Gravitational energy-momentum trace decoupling and resolution of the vacuum energy catastrophe.

title: "Mind the Gap: Generative AI and the Context Problem in Software Architecture Practice - Interview Guideline"
abstract: "Use of generative AI (GenAI) in domains such as softwaredevelopment, healthcare, or finance is becoming the norm. Potential advantagesfor software architecture are also clear: automate routine tasks, explore solutionspaces, and even challenge design assumptions. The reality, however, is morenuanced and poses a question: how do software architects actually use it andwhere does it fall short? We conducted semi-structured interviews with tensoftware architects at a large industrial company and applied a coding processinspired by grounded theory to analyze the results. The core observation is thatGenAI is already well-accepted for mechanical tasks but is rarely used forhigh-context judgments that underpin the architecture work. Interestingly, thebottleneck is rarely the GenAI models, but rather the missing project-awareintegration layer that connects the models to the architect\u2019s real world of scattereddocumentation, legacy code, and governance constraints. Based on thesefindings, we outline implications for tool builders, team leads, and individualarchitects. In this dataset, we provide the interview template."

title: Cross-Water Acoustic Domain Adaptation Is Direction-Dependent: A Four-Corpus UDA Benchmark with Negative Transfer
abstract: Underwater acoustic target recognition (UATR) models trained on one body of water can fail to generalize to another, and unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) is a widely used remedy when the target water has no labels. We benchmark four UDA paradigms—source-only training, correlation alignment (CORAL), multi-kernel MMD, and domain-adversarial training (DANN, CDAN)—against a target-only supervised reference on a frozen two-class protocol spanning four corpora: the Strait-of-Georgia marine corpus Oceanship, freshwater-lake QiandaoEar22, an AIS-auto-labeled VTUAD reconstruction, and nearshore ShipsEar (40 method–direction combinations; ten seeds on the two-domain matrix and eight on the seven extension directions, 344 runs in total; strict source-validation model selection, exploratory paired significance tests; DANN/CDAN on the two-domain matrix only). We use “target oracle” solely as shorthand for this target-only supervised reference under the present architecture and protocol; it is not a theoretical upper bound. Under this protocol, adaptation can work but is strongly direction-asymmetric. In the lake→ocean (QiandaoEar22→Oceanship) direction, MMD lifts macro-F1 from 0.359 (near-total source-only collapse onto the majority class) to 0.524 ± 0.090, recovering 74% of the target-only supervised reference, and restoring passenger-ship recall from at most 9/1,214 on any source-only seed to 662/1,214 on the best-macro-F1 seed; all four UDA methods improve over source-only significantly, while pairwise differences among the UDA methods remain unresolved. In the ocean→lake (Oceanship→QiandaoEar22) direction the target-only oracle itself is low (0.551 macro-F1 with an 89-segment minority test class), indicating limited supervised headroom under the present architecture, labels, and split; there UDA’s measurable value is accuracy-variance compression (variance ratios 0.044–0.376 vs. source-only) and class-bias correction. On the two-domain matrix the most stable method in each direction is a moment-matching method (CORAL lake→ocean, MMD ocean→lake) and the least stable an adversarial one; the conditional variant CDAN exhibits a direction-dependent early-stopping collapse, with three of ten seeds frozen at epoch 1. The VTUAD third domain reverses the moment-matching ranking—CORAL shows fewer severe observed degradations than MMD across the evaluated directions and leads the only VTUAD direction with significant adaptation gains (QiandaoEar22→VTUAD, +0.129, p = 0.0008)—and MMD produces a significant negative adaptation (VTUAD→QiandaoEar22, −0.147 macro-F1, p = 0.005). On the hardest ShipsEar direction, none of the evaluated source-only/CORAL/MMD methods achieved a useful macro-F1 under this protocol (≤ 0.194 vs. a 0.8356 majority-class baseline). No method dominated across all directions, indicating that transfer direction and target-domain constraints are stronger determinants of performance than a universal choice of UDA objective. Recording/clip-level re-aggregation is reported as a three-seed robustness analysis because per-segment predictions were archived for the initial batch only; the primary multi-seed comparisons remain segment-level under recording/clip-disjoint splits. We release the MMSI-retaining VTUAD pipeline, code, frozen splits, and per-seed results.

title: Rabi profile framework: A simple analytical and graphical toolkit for quantum control
abstract: We introduce the Rabi profile, the Rabi spectrum, and the Rabi leak as triad of mathematically rigorous but conceptually transparent quantum-control tools that provide a framework for assessing the feasibility and selectivity of coherent state control in quantum systems with arbitrarily many levels, without recourse to numerical simulation. As the rigorous foundation for this framework, we present a self-contained discussion of the rotating wave approximation (RWA) and its limits, suitable for use as classroom material. We illustrate its practical utility by application to design of superconducting transmon qubits. Because it reduces complex quantum control questions to elementary frequency-domain reasoning, the Rabi profile framework is intended to serve equally as a research diagnostic and as a pedagogical bridge between introductory quantum mechanics and contemporary quantum technologies.

title: Common-mode rejection with a robust LOCC benchmark for four gravitationally coupled oscillators
abstract: Removing a common displacement from a gravitational channel test need not preserve its ability to exclude classical communication between quantum laboratories. We give a quantitative construction for four oscillators in a passive Newtonian rotating-wave model, using independent unknown coherent inputs, local heterodyne measurements, and classical subtraction of the common mode. An analytic bound on a bounded score holds for every normal local-operations-and-classical-communication (LOCC) channel, without an output-energy or Gaussian restriction. The ideal quantum mean is 0.125, whereas the LOCC mean is below 0.124068. With residual gain errors of 0.1%, phase errors of 0.01 radians, and an independently bounded common displacement, the respective bounds remain above 0.124581 and below 0.124438. We exhibit a common-noise regime in which the original vacuum-outcome criterion loses its guarantee while the relative score retains one. A conservative fixed-sample test controls false exclusion with memory in the null. The result assumes quantum local matter and trusted measurement structure; it neither excludes all classical phase-space models nor establishes experimental feasibility. This record contains the preprint, editable LaTeX source, and an offline reproducibility archive with exact-arithmetic certificates and 26 computational tests. One project-history test requiring undistributed literature copies is explicitly excluded from the public runner. Substantial use of generative AI is disclosed in the manuscript. This preprint has not undergone journal peer review. title: Continuous Novel Discovery: The Minimum Configuration for Artificial Superintelligence
abstract: Every existing definition of artificial superintelligence (ASI) inherits an unmeasurable baseline —the upper limit of human cognitive ability. We propose a definition that avoids this dependency:ASI is continuous novel discovery, a self-sustaining loop in which a system expands its knowledgespace by discovering what was not known, updating its own representations, and moving to thenext unknown, without termination. We formalize this as an infinite sequence of verified strictexpansions of a knowledge state, and distinguish three tiers of novelty by whether the expansionadds content within a fixed representational space (Tiers 1 and 2) or enlarges the space itself(Tier 3). We identify a five-component minimum configuration for the loop — a T3-capablecognitive layer, a physical verification layer, a knowledge-space update mechanism, a directionmechanism, and a cross-domain propagation system — formalize the components as operatorsin a state-transition system, and argue that each is necessary: removing any one yields a systemthat already exists — the AI Scientist, A-Lab, Hakken, the Robot Scientist, or standard LLMinference — whose documented limitations are traceable to the missing component. We evaluatesix current AI discovery systems against this specification and find that none satisfies all fivecomponents, though several achieve genuine results within Tier 1. We propose Experiment as aService (EaaS) as the architecture that closes the physical-verification loop, building on existingclosed-loop infrastructures in pharmaceutical screening and self-driving laboratories, and providea technology inventory identifying what exists and what is missing. No fundamental scientificbreakthrough appears to be required; the distance from the current state to a minimally functionalsystem is engineering, not science.

title: LSG: A Lightweight Supervised Gate for Sub-Millisecond Agentic Memory Novelty Filtering
abstract: This paper presents LSG (Lightweight Supervised Gate), a shallow calibrated ensemble architecture for write-time memory novelty filtering in long-horizon LLM agents. Contemporary agentic memory systems rely on cosine similarity thresholds for filtering incoming conversational turns — a heuristic that suffers from O(N) computational scaling, single-turn context blindness, and miscalibrated confidence estimates. LSG addresses these structural limitations by combining frozen 384-dimensional Sentence-BERT embeddings, multi-turn context history windowing (K=2), conversational metadata features, Platt probability calibration, and a 2nd-stage Logistic Regression Meta-Learner. Evaluated zero-shot on the PersonaChat benchmark (1,600 turns) against gold-standard human intent labels verified via LLM-as-a-Judge (κ = 0.84), LSG achieves competitive discriminative ranking (AUPRC = 0.569, ROC-AUC = 0.566) while executing in constant O(1) time at 0.15 ms on CPU — over 500× faster than Small Language Model alternatives such as Qwen2.5-0.5B and Llama-3.2-1B, and eliminating the memory bloat caused by degenerate pass-through heuristics. Keywords: agentic memory, memory write gating, LLM agents, Platt calibration, multi-turn context, Pareto efficiency, lightweight classifiers, RAG, conversational AI

title: LLM Usage in Russia — 2026
abstract: A unified estimate of weekly and daily users of eleven generative AI chat services in Russia (population aged 12+, Q2 2026), with task structure and user profiles, based on open data from Mediascope, VCIOM, OMI, Yandex, Similarweb and other sources. 48.6 million people, 40% of Russia's population aged 12+, use generative AI chats every week; 67.9 million (56%) monthly; 12.9 million (10.6%, model estimate) daily. Yandex's Alice AI leads with 30.9 million weekly users, 3.7 times ChatGPT (8.2 million). Russian services account for 63% of the aggregate weekly audience of the eleven services, US services for 24%, Chinese services for 12%. A weekly Alice AI user sends about 5 requests a week; a weekly ChatGPT user worldwide sends about 25 messages. People under 25 make up 17% of the population aged 12+ and 43% of the daily AI audience. The record contains the Russian original and an English translation (web version: geoboost.pro/en/research/llm-russia). The report documents the reconciliation method (methods A, B and V), numbered assumptions (appendix A) and 63 sources (appendix B). Machine-readable estimates are in the linked dataset.

title: Fairness-aware artificial intelligence tutoring for multilingual learners: evaluating adaptive feedback across L1 and proficiency groups
abstract: Introduction Recent advances in large language models (LLMs), such as GPT-4, have created new opportunities for intelligent computer-assisted language learning, particularly through personalized feedback for multilingual English learners. Building on research in automated writing evaluation (AWE), this study developed an equity-aware AI tutoring framework that integrates GPT-generated feedback with rule-based simulated feedback for learner spelling errors. The framework draws on annotated TOEFL-Spell data enriched with learner first-language (L1) and English proficiency information to examine feedback quality, accessibility, personalization, and potential subgroup disparities. Methods A verified matched analysis of 32 complete GPT-simulated feedback pairs was conducted using feedback length, Flesch Reading Ease, BERTScore, non-parametric subgroup tests, paired comparisons, effect-size estimates, and exploratory regression models controlling for selected input characteristics. Results GPT-generated feedback demonstrated substantial semantic correspondence with simulated feedback, achieving an overall BERTScore precision of 0.8370, recall of 0.8742, and F1 score of 0.8552. GPT feedback was significantly longer than simulated feedback ( M = 608.12 vs. 218.69 characters, p < 0.001) and, contrary to the preliminary analysis, was also significantly more readable on average ( M = 75.62 vs. 64.64, p < 0.001). GPT feedback length did not differ significantly across L1 ( p = 0.143) or proficiency groups ( p = 0.422), while GPT readability showed a significant omnibus difference across proficiency levels ( p = 0.047); however, no pairwise comparison remained significant after Holm correction. BERTScore F1 was stable across both L1 ( p = 0.775) and proficiency groups ( p = 0.500). Exploratory controlled analyses likewise provided no consistent evidence that L1 independently predicted feedback readability or semantic alignment after accounting for prompt and error characteristics. Discussion Accordingly, observed subgroup variation is interpreted as descriptive heterogeneity rather than definitive evidence of algorithmic or sociolinguistic bias. Because L1 and proficiency were not fully crossed in the analytical sample, their independent effects could not be completely disentangled. A Gradio-based interface ( https://huggingface.co/spaces/Oluyori/equity-ai-tutor ) was additionally developed to demonstrate the practical deployment of the tutoring framework. The findings demonstrate LLM-based feedback potential for semantically aligned and accessible language support while emphasizing the need for larger, balanced samples, learner-centered evaluation, and multidimensional fairness assessment before claims regarding equitable educational performance can be made.

title: Permutation-Lifted Hypergraph Product Codes for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing: GF(2)-Native Construction with Reduced Stabiliser Weight and Improved Simulated Threshold
abstract: We introduce the Permutation-Lifted Hypergraph Product (PL-HGP) code family, a GF(2)-native generalisation of the Tillich–Zemor hypergraph product (HGP) construction based on the XOR permutation lift Ḣ₂ := H₂⊕H₂Π, where Π is a girth-maximising column permutation and ⊕ denotes bitwise GF(2) addition. We prove that PL-HGP codes preserve the [[n, k₁k₂, min(d₁,d₂)]] parameters of standard HGP codes and that the XOR lift reduces the maximum stabiliser weight Δₘₐˣ, providing a mechanistic explanation for the simulated threshold improvement. Through Monte Carlo simulation (Stim [57] + PyMatching [31], ≥10⁵ logical failures per point), the corrected simulated threshold is pₜₕ = (1.07±0.04)% at d = 9 under circuit-level depolarising noise and (2.41±0.05)% under biased Pauli noise, exceeding the symmetric HGP simulation baseline by 0.13 pp. Physical-qubit overhead benchmarks show a 23–28% reduction relative to symmetric HGP across d∈{5,…,17} (Table IV). Simulation studies across three hardware-calibrated noise models (superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic) show threshold consistency within ±0.09 pp, motivating future cross-platform hardware experiments. A proposed FPGA-based MWPM decoder architecture, evaluated at synthesis level on a Xilinx VU13P at 400 MHz, projects 91µs latency at d = 15 (synthesis-level estimate; physical FPGA implementation required to confirm). All results are fully reproducible using the open-source Stim and PyMatching tools.

title: I Prove, Therefore I Am: Spatiotemporal Multi-Party Computation
abstract: Secure multiparty computation (MPC) enables mutually distrustful parties to compute on private digital inputs. We initiate the study of spatiotemporal MPC, extending this paradigm to functionalities whose inputs additionally depend on physical facts such as the parties' locations, times, or trajectories. Such protocols must simultaneously hide spatiotemporal information and ensure its physical consistency: a malicious party should not be able to make the functionality operate on a spatiotemporal input inconsistent with its actual physical state. The main conceptual challenge is to formulate extraction of spatiotemporal information within the simulation-based security framework. We introduce arguments of spatiotemporal knowledge, following the principle "I prove, therefore I am:" rather than defining physical presence directly through a mathematical relation, we define it operationally through the ability to complete a sound spatiotemporal verification protocol. Accordingly, an extractor recovers a spatiotemporal point from a successful prover and certifies its physical validity by using the extracted prover to succeed in an auxiliary spatiotemporal verification protocol. Building on this notion, we define universally composable (UC) security for spatiotemporal MPC, capturing privacy, physical consistency, and composability. We provide constructions achieving this new MPC notion. We first construct UC-secure commit-and-prove of spatiotemporal knowledge: in the CRS model under LWE against quantum provers without pre-shared entanglement, and in the QROM against quantum provers with unbounded pre-shared entanglement. Using these protocols, we obtain UC-secure spatiotemporal MPC from semi-honest post-quantum MPC. We also extend our framework to support quantum functionalities with classical spatiotemporal input.

title: MICRO: Multi-Fidelity Active Search for Severe Error Discovery
abstract: Human feedback can vary in cost and informativeness. Strong feedback can reveal severe errors but is costly, so cheaper quality ratings can help decide which items to annotate. We propose MICRO (Multi-Fidelity Impact Clustered Rollout), an active search framework that allocates a shared budget to these feedback types to maximise confirmed severe error discoveries. MICRO jointly models ratings and annotation losses conditional on item features to steer acquisition. It clusters acquisitions by their predicted impact on severity probabilities to select diverse candidates, then uses rollout to estimate their discovery value. Experiments on WMT20 English-German show that ratings improve both loss reconstruction and severity prediction. MICRO achieves the highest mean discovery count across four budget and rating cost settings, with similar performance to adapted MF-ENS in one and significant gains over all six comparison policies, including two rollout controls, in the other three $(p<.001)$.

title: Calibration Is Not Verification: Falsifiability-Aware Conformal Routing for Mixture-of-Agents
abstract: Multi-agent language systems often treat agreement as evidence, yet heterogeneous agents can jointly repeat an unsupported claim or omit a correct specialist fact. We introduce C-MoA, an agreement-based conformal filter that turns inter-agent semantic support into a claim-level nonconformity score and calibrates a retention threshold at the example level, giving distribution-free within-domain factuality control for heterogeneous Mixture-of-Agents. C-MoA is effective: it nearly doubles retained-claim precision on long-form generation (from 0.41 to 0.75), certifies a human-labelled medical set, and transfers across domains without recalibration; its one failure mode is short-form answering, where consensus is cheap and the score is left near chance. We then ask whether counterfactual falsifiability can push past consensus, and introduce CONTRA-MoA, which adds a blinded near-miss tournament, leave-one-agent-out stability, and availability-aware fusion. This extension helps only where the verifier holds domain knowledge, dropping half of the false medical claims at 0.940 precision, whereas with a memory-only judge the added signals are near chance (AUC 0.531 and 0.511) and naive max fusion degrades the working agreement signal from 0.687 to 0.652. The message is twofold: agreement-based conformal calibration delivers reliable, transferable factuality control, while moving beyond consensus requires a knowledgeable verifier, availability-aware signals, and robust fusion.

title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Modern Pretrained Encoders for Low-Resource Entity-Level Financial Sentiment Classification
abstract: Financial news may express different sentiments towards the entities it mentions, while labelled examples for entity-level classification are often limited. This study compares the adaptation of three pretrained encoders to this task on FinEntity: FinBERT, a model based on Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) and further pretrained on financial text; DeBERTa-v3-base, the base-sized third version of Decoding-enhanced BERT with disentangled attention; and ModernBERT-base, a modern bidirectional Transformer encoder. Term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features with a linear support vector machine (SVM) serve as the traditional baseline. The pretrained encoders use explicit target-entity markers and a representation combining global and entity information. Three adaptation strategies are considered: full fine-tuning, a frozen encoder and low-rank adaptation (LoRA). Evaluation covers overall classification performance, trainable parameter counts, learning with reduced training data, variation across random seeds, entity representation and transfer to another dataset. In the overall comparison, FinBERT and DeBERTa-v3-base outperform the traditional baseline, whereas ModernBERT-base does not. DeBERTa-v3-base obtains the highest macro-averaged F1 score (Macro-F1) in this comparison. FinBERT performs better at the smallest training budget and produces more consistent results across the tested seeds, indicating that the preferred encoder depends on the evaluation setting. LoRA achieves competitive classification scores with only a small proportion of parameters updated, although this reduction does not shorten training time in the reported experiments. Combining global and target-entity representations improves performance for both encoders evaluated in the ablation study. Without further fine-tuning, the two LoRA models also achieve Macro-F1 scores above 0.70 on SEntFiN, but both score lower than on FinEntity. The results support parameter-efficient adaptation for this task while showing that performance under limited data, consistency across runs and transfer to another dataset require separate consideration.

title: PathQ-Former: a missing-modality audit of histology-transcriptomics survival models and a one-checkpoint training recipe
abstract: Code, configurations, archived per-run results (180 five-fold runs on five TCGA cohorts) and the experimental report for PathQ-Former, a Q-Former-style fusion model of whole-slide-image patch embeddings (UNI2-h) and RNA-seq pathway tokens that predicts discrete-time survival hazards and keeps working when either modality is missing. Under an identical fixed-budget protocol it improves the C-index over the official SurvPath implementation by +0.037 pooled over 75 paired folds (paired t p = 0.002). Trained checkpoints are on the HuggingFace Hub (sharoonsharif1/PathQFormer-checkpoints).

title: Microsoft® Windows® 11 DNS Client and HTTPS Session Behavior
abstract: An observational examination of DNS-mediated resolution, HTTPS transport establishment, and application-layer session persistence within Windows® 11.The study correlates resolver state, transport continuity, session transitions, and asynchronous application events across overlapping temporal states.Particular attention is given to non-synchronous transitions between network reachability and higher-order session behavior.Observed relationships are documented without assigning causality, fault, intent, or security significance beyond the available evidence.

title: Intentions to use Robo-tour guides at cultural heritage sites: Role of Speciesism and Anthropomorphism
abstract: Objectives: To explore the cognitive and emotional factors influencing tourists' acceptance of robot guides in cultural heritage sites, specifically examining the impact of anthropomorphism, ease of use, innovativeness, and design attributes, alongside the mediating roles of intellectual intelligence and speciesism. Methods: A dual methodology combining Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) was applied to data collected from 418 tourists who interacted with robot guides. Results: Anthropomorphism and ease of use significantly predict usage intention, whereas personal innovativeness lacks a direct effect. Intellectual intelligence and speciesism fully mediate these relationships. Furthermore, NCA identifies critical design thresholds for high acceptance: at least 50% anthropomorphism and 62.7% intellectual intelligence. Ultimately, relational and cognitive factors drive usage intentions more than purely functional attributes. Conclusions: This study advances heritage tourism and human-robot interaction literature by highlighting speciesism as a critical mediator. Identifying specific design thresholds provides developers and cultural site managers with actionable guidelines to optimize robot acceptance by balancing emotional and cognitive elements, while opening avenues for future cross-cultural validation.

title: Attempts to investigate what words trivia experts focus on in quiz questions: Human-AI comparison through “LLM-as-a-judge” approach
abstract: Computational capacity and knowledge of humans are more limited than those of large language models (LLMs). However, in buzzer quizzes, human trivia experts can often identify the correct answer even from insufficient information such as only a few words. Investigating how they can make fast and accurate judgments is expected to highlight new characteristics of human intelligence, but little is known about that. In this exploratory and case-based analysis, we predicted that trivia experts and LLMs would differ in which words/phrases in a question are important for identifying the answer, and compared experts' performance with LLMs' performance in Japanese trivia questions through an LLM-as-a-judge approach: We regarded LLMs as evaluators and then used their outputs as comparative tools for experts' evaluations. First, we constructed a quiz question processing system that tokenized question texts based on morphological analysis and then numerically evaluated the importance of each token using GPT-4o/GPT-4.1. Then, we conducted a behavioral experiment wherein actual trivia experts were asked to numerically evaluate the importance of each token, just as LLMs had performed. As a result, trivia experts treated a variety of words/phrases as important, even if each word/phrase did not appear to be strongly associated with the answer. Their evaluation scores tended to accumulate faster than those of the LLMs. This may indicate that trivia experts can make inductive inferences faster (e.g., finding a common concept even from few items). More advanced question-answering systems may be designed by applying trivia experts' cognitive processes to LLMs' information processing, and our findings may provide a scaffolding toward such goals.

title: A reproducible protocol for auditing XAI-based trading policies: A case study on the S&P/BVL Peru General Index
abstract: Explainability methods increasingly inform real-time trading interventions, but claims of “behavioral correction” in this literature are rarely tested under the chronological separation, ablation, and multiplicity control that such claims require. We introduce a reproducible audit protocol — explicit train/validation/test roles with next-label embargoes, validation-only hyperparameter selection, close- t to open- t + 1 execution, an explainability-ablated baseline, a temporal permutation control, and bootstrap/multiplicity-corrected uncertainty — and apply it as a stress test to a previously reported CXAI-Guided Dynamic Stop-Loss (CGDSL) case study (3244 daily S&P/BVL Peru General Index observations, 2011–2024). Under this protocol, an originally reported “topological proof” of behavioral correction (Hazard Ratio sign change, 90.6% bias-mass reduction, 0% false-alarm rate) does not survive: adjusted tests are null under both within-seed and pooled 30-test multiplicity control, paired intervals reach zero, and two of three matched interventions produce counterfactual harm. Two post-review extensions probe the explainability component directly, with mixed results: an ATR-only ablation that removes the attribution gate achieves a more disciplined descriptive BDI than the full policy in two of three seeds, yet CGDSL’s net PnL exceeds the ablated baseline’s in all three seeds; and a temporal permutation of the attribution signal places the observed BDI at the 0.4th–3.8th percentile of an unadjusted null distribution, a diagnostic we report as exploratory rather than confirmatory. We argue the protocol’s value lies precisely in surfacing such mixed, unglamorous findings rather than only favorable ones, and offer it as a template other XAI-trading audits can apply before, not after, publication.

title: The Most Informative Bit and Beyond: A Proof of the Courtade--Kumar Conjecture and Multibit Extensions
abstract: Let \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) be uniform on the Boolean cube, and let \(Y\) be obtained by passing its coordinates independently through a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability \(p\). For a \(k\)-bit quantizer \(Q(X)\), reporting \(k\) input coordinates retains \(k(1-h_2(p))\) bits of information, making coordinate projections a natural quantization benchmark. For \(k=1\), this is the Courtade--Kumar conjecture: every Boolean function \(f\) satisfies \(I(f(X);Y)\leq 1-h_2(p)\), with equality for coordinate functions. We prove the conjecture in every dimension and for every crossover probability, without a balance assumption. The proof tracks the information gap relative to a coordinate as the channel correlation varies. After a monotone rearrangement, an entropy-flow identity relates the derivative of this gap to the edge boundary of the associated Boolean decision set. A sharp local entropy comparison, Fourier analysis, and logarithmic Sobolev estimates for pivotal sets imply that any positive gap must grow as the noise decreases, contradicting its nonpositive value at the noiseless endpoint. For \(k\geq8\), a coding-theoretic phenomenon emerges. We construct a shortened-Hamming-code quantizer that beats the coordinate benchmark for \(k=8\), and a direct-sum argument extends the failure to every \(k\geq8\). Thus structured coding can retain more information than coordinate selection. Exhaustive searches within several structured code families and Monte Carlo searches over random codebooks for \(2\leq k\leq7\) find that structured codebooks outperform random ones but remain below the coordinate benchmark. This motivates our conjecture that coordinate projections are optimal for \(2\leq k\leq7\).

title: Affine Symmetries of Polynomial Roots with Multiplicities and Applications to Constacyclic Codes
abstract: Let $f(X)$ be a polynomial over a finite field, and let its defining function record the multiplicities of its roots. In this paper, we introduce the affine stabilizer group and the affine stabilizer group scheme of the defining function of $f(X)$. These objects characterize the affine symmetries of the roots of $f(X)$ together with their multiplicities. We establish structural descriptions of these affine stabilizers and relate them to the coefficient structure of $f(X)$. In particular, the affine stabilizer group determines quotient structures of the defining function, which yield canonical descriptions of the corresponding semi-invariant polynomial spaces. The resulting coefficient constraints provide explicit restrictions on the possible supports of polynomials with prescribed affine symmetries. The affine stabilizer group scheme further captures infinitesimal symmetries arising from multiple roots and gives refined coefficient constraints beyond those obtained from ordinary affine transformations. We apply this framework to generator polynomials of constacyclic codes over finite fields. The affine stabilizer structure of a generator polynomial induces subcodes defined by semi-invariant conditions and provides constraints on their dimensions and Hamming distances. In the special case of multiplicative symmetries, the construction specializes to the support-primitive decomposition of constacyclic codes.

title: Risk Prediction in Cash-in-Transit Security Using Machine Learning: A Data-Driven Performance Evaluations
abstract: Cash-in-transit (CIT) transactions are the transportation of banknotes and cash between ATMs, cash processing centers, banks and retailer locations. Robbery, route compromise, leaking of information from inside the group, vehicle attacks, abnormal dwell times, and unsafe route deviations are all rare but high-impact threats that are faced during these trips. title: Environment-Context Manipulation of Authorisation Adjudication in Autonomous LLM Agents
abstract: An empirical measurement study of how planted environment text affects an autonomous offensive-security agent's authorisation decisions, and of how far those effects survive a change of model, of sample size, and of the attacker's own knowledge. Status: pre-submission archive. The apparatus and data are complete for the results reported here; two follow-up controls (an attacker brief with no pre-granted authorisation framing, and a forged notice carrying source authority) are planned and not yet run. Known limitations and corrections are listed explicitly in docs/REANALYSIS.md and docs/CLAIM-AUDIT.md. Contents: the measurement harness (src/asi_bench/), a deployable defensive component (src/asi_deploy/), all per-run records behind every reported number (data/), and the project's own failure log (docs/FINDINGS.md). All statistics can be recomputed offline without calling a model.

title: Monotonic Analytic Wavelet Front-Ends with Dynamic Non-Stationary Adaptation for Raw-Waveform Speaker Recognition
abstract: This work introduces a learnable, fully differentiable raw-waveform front-end designed to overcome the rigid time-frequency trade-offs of fixed Short-Time Fourier Transforms (STFT) as well as the sample inefficiency, parameter bloat, and phase vulnerabilities of unconstrained 1D temporal convolutions. The proposed architecture parameterizes an analytic Gabor filterbank governed by three physical inductive biases: (1) a cumulative softmax reparameterization that guarantees strictly monotonic center frequency allocation, entirely preventing filter crossover, harmonic clustering, and spectral dead zones; (2) an analytic Constant-Q temporal scaling constraint coupled with Hilbert quadrature carrier decomposition to extract instantaneous amplitude envelopes without zero-crossing phase cancellation; and (3) a lightweight temporal context module that dynamically modulates channel-wise gains to adapt to non-stationary acoustic bursts and vocal-tract dynamics. When integrated into an ECAPA-TDNN backbone and optimized with Additive Angular Margin Softmax (ArcFace), the proposed front-end reduces verification error from 5.40% to 3.90% Equal Error Rate (EER)—a 27.8% relative error reduction—over a matched unconstrained 1D convolutional baseline on LibriSpeech verification trials, while reducing the core filter receptive field parameters by over 99.5% (128 versus 25,664 weights).

title: Post-Generation Response Transformation Against Unauthorized Model Distillation: An Empirical Case Study
abstract: Unauthorized model distillation creates a growing security problem for language-model providers: an attacker can collect API responses at scale and use them as supervision for a smaller local model. This work investigates a deployment-separable defense in which the protected teacher model remains unchanged while an external, risk-gated layer transforms the visible response after generation. The study examines two prototype approaches. ITRO applies adaptive, domain-aware reasoning obfuscation, while SPECTRE introduces a more consistent false-start structure intended to reduce the training value of collected reasoning traces. On the finalized GSM8K evaluation, the clean-distillation student achieved 39.6% accuracy, the ITRO student 39.0%, the SPECTRE student 34.8%, and a no-rationale student 37.0%. The recorded average training losses were 0.1637 for clean training, 0.2555 for ITRO, and 0.3512 for SPECTRE. These results are descriptive rather than definitive: the experiments consist of single historical runs, and the observed degradation has not yet been replicated across seeds, harder benchmarks, or adaptive attackers. The findings nevertheless suggest that post-generation transformation remains a useful research direction, particularly if future methods can preserve natural and semantically correct explanations for legitimate users while systematically reducing their value as distillation supervision. The work therefore motivates further research on semantic verification, adaptive sanitization, human utility, reproducibility, and the economics of response-layer anti-distillation defenses.

title: PAKT: Physically-Aligned Kinesthetic Teaching for Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) systems still struggle with the demands of contact-rich industrial manipulation, including micrometer-level precision, success rates above 99%, and human-level cycle times. Although off-policy algorithms can improve performance by leveraging demonstrations and interventions, a key bottleneck is the lack of an intuitive interface for collecting such guidance while complying with constraints of the physical system and the policy. We propose PAKT, a framework for kinesthetic teaching in RL. As opposed to teleoperation approaches, PAKT relies on kinesthetic guidance, which is widely used in industry. However, a critical weakness of kinesthetic guidance is the possibility for the operator to move the robot along trajectories (e.g., velocities, accelerations, jerk) that the robot and/or policy cannot physically reproduce. Using PAKT, operators guide the robot through admittance control, which maps human-applied forces to motion. The downstream reference generator applies the same kinematic limits used during policy execution, keeping the collected trajectories within these limits. To support this teaching interface with an appropriate execution layer, PAKT adds a high-performance control stack that maps low-frequency RL actions to high-frequency torque commands. It consists of a reference generator and subsequent impedance controller, where the reference generator preserves the tracking performance of the impedance controller while improving contact handling and producing smoother policy actions. Across the reported runs on four insertion and industrial assembly benchmarks, including a data center compute tray, the end-to-end system reduces cycle time by 23%-48% and cumulative intervention count by 62%-86% relative to the HIL-SERL baseline. title: Formal verification of tilt estimation using the Rocq prover
abstract: The safe operation of a humanoid robot critically relies on accurate estimation of its vertical orientation, or ``tilt''. This requires a variety of mathematical tools, including three-dimensional geometry and differential equations. To formally verify tilt estimation, we develop a library for stability analysis in the Rocq prover. We start by formalizing a theory of ordinary differential equations. We provide a formalization of the (local) Cauchy-Lipschitz (a.k.a. Picard-Lindelof) theorem for existence and uniqueness, taking advantage of the library support for quotients provided by the Mathematical Components library. We extend this formalization with a variant for global existence and continuous dependence on initial conditions. Building on these foundations, we develop a theory of Lyapunov stability that is compatible with an existing formalization of LaSalle's invariance principle. We also extend an existing library for the statics of robot manipulators to support dynamical systems. Finally, we apply these libraries to the verification of a state-of-the-art tilt estimation developed for a humanoid robot.

title: SMTB: Fast Structure-Mapping with Tight Bounds
abstract: Structure-mapping forms analogies by aligning systems of relationally connected elements based on shared structure instead of surface features. We introduce a new structure-mapping algorithm: Structure-Mapping with Tight Bounds (SMTB) that is 5--15x faster than the structure-mapping engine (SME) and about 50\% better at finding mappings in large nested domains. SMTB is part of the broader Cognitive Rule Engine (CRE) project, a flexible multi-language-compatible framework with an accessible Python interface to state-of-the-art C++ implementations of core algorithms commonly used in cognitive systems such as pattern matching, planning, and structure-mapping. CRE and SMTB are designed to work with a wide range of representation choices. Unlike SME, which biases higher-order correspondences in tree-like predicate logic, SMTB maximizes relational connectivity without privileging higher-order relations. This allows SMTB to work just as well over arbitrary relational graphs as it does in tree-like domains of nested predicate logic. We discuss situations where privileging "higher-orderness" in structure-mapping can cause issues, and illustrate how SMTB avoids failure modes that SME would encounter in these situations. We also provide an evaluation comparing SMTB to SME v4 over 5845 domain pairs from the SME corpus.

evidence.title: SMTB: Fast Structure-Mapping with Tight Bounds
evidence.abstract: Structure-mapping forms analogies by aligning systems of relationally connected elements based on shared structure instead of surface features. We introduce a new structure-mapping algorithm: Structure-Mapping with Tight Bounds (SMTB) that is 5--15x faster than the structure-mapping engine (SME) and about 50\% better at finding mappings in large nested domains. SMTB is part of the broader Cognitive Rule Engine (CRE) project, a flexible multi-language-compatible framework with an accessible Python interface to state-of-the-art C++ implementations of core algorithms commonly used in cognitive systems such as pattern matching, planning, and structure-mapping. CRE and SMTB are designed to work with a wide range of representation choices. Unlike SME, which biases higher-order correspondences in tree-like predicate logic, SMTB maximizes relational connectivity without privileging higher-order relations. This allows SMTB to work just as well over arbitrary relational graphs as it does in tree-like domains of nested predicate logic. We discuss situations where privileging "higher-orderness" in structure-mapping can cause issues, and illustrate how SMTB avoids failure modes that SME would encounter in these situations. We also provide an evaluation comparing SMTB to SME v4 over 5845 domain pairs from the SME corpus.

title: Mitigating overconfidence in nonlinear Kalman filters via covariance recalibration
abstract: The Kalman filter (KF) is an optimal linear state estimator for linear systems, and numerous extensions, including the extended Kalman filter (EKF), unscented Kalman filter (UKF), and cubature Kalman filter (CKF), have been developed for nonlinear systems. Although these nonlinear KFs differ in how they approximate nonlinear transformations, they all retain the same update framework as the linear KF. In this paper, we show that, under nonlinear measurements, this conventional framework inherently tends to underestimate the true posterior covariance, leading to overconfident covariance estimates. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to provide a mathematical proof of this systematic covariance underestimation in a general nonlinear KF framework. Motivated by this analysis, we propose a covariance-recalibrated framework that re-approximates the measurement model after the state update to better capture the actual effect of the Kalman gain on the posterior covariance; when recalibration indicates that an update is harmful, the update can be withdrawn. The proposed framework can be combined with essentially any existing nonlinear KF, and simulations across four nonlinear KFs and five applications show that it substantially improves both state and covariance estimation accuracy, often reducing errors by several orders of magnitude. The code and supplementary material are available at https://github.com/Shida-Jiang/A-new-framework-for-nonlinear-Kalman-filters .

title: Axis-Specific, Dose-Dependent, and Direction-Dependent Output Responses to Transformer Representation Interventions
abstract: A representation direction can explain a large share of hidden-state variance without necessarily producing a large change in model output when the hidden state is perturbed along it. Paper 1 established that multilingual BERT’s [MASK]-position hidden states at layer L11 contain six reproducible representation axes, C0–C5, defined by singular value decomposition, but deliberately made no claims about their functional consequences. The present study tests those consequences directly, using controlled additive activation intervention (h' = h + αv) at the same L11 representation (model.bert.encoder.layer[11] output, equivalently hidden_states[12]) and the same canonical C0–C5 directions. We intervene across 400 controlled contextual inputs (Japanese, English, numerical, symbolic; 100 each), six axes (C0–C5), and eight intervention strengths (α ∈ {−8, −4, −2, −1, 1, 2, 4, 8}), yielding 19,200 axis-intervention conditions. As a control, we independently sample six random unit directions (R0–R5) in the same 768-dimensional space and intervene with the same procedure at α ∈ {−8, −4, −2, 2, 4, 8}, yielding 14,400 random-direction conditions, for 33,600 conditions in total. Output change is measured by KL divergence between baseline and intervened next-token probability distributions at the [MASK] position, alongside JS divergence, logit cosine similarity, and logit L2 distance. Aggregate mean KL divergence differs substantially across axes: C0 (0.813) > C2 (0.372) ≈ C1 (0.364) > C3 (0.260) > C4 (0.154) > C5 (0.135). Compared against pooled random-direction responses at matched intervention strengths, C0–C3 show significantly larger output change than random directions (Mann–Whitney p from 1.6×10⁻¹⁹⁹ to 9.6×10⁻⁹⁰, Cohen’s d from 0.57 to 1.21), while C4 and C5 do not differ significantly from the pooled random baseline. A complementary stream-matched comparison, in which each axis is compared only to its own matched independent random direction, tells a partly different story: C0–C4 all exceed their matched random stream significantly, while C5 falls slightly below its matched random stream. This discrepancy between the pooled and stream-matched comparisons is itself a substantive finding, and we report both without resolving them into a single ranking. All six axes show a strong, statistically significant monotonic dose-response relationship between |α| and output change (Spearman ρ = 0.87–0.94, all p < 0.001). Four axes (C0, C2, C3, C4) show a consistent directional asymmetry in which negative-sign intervention produces larger output change than positive-sign intervention of equal magnitude; C1 shows the asymmetry in the opposite direction; C5 shows no significant asymmetry. All six axes show significant category dependence (Kruskal–Wallis p < 0.001), but the category that elicits the largest response differs by axis (C0 and C1: symbolic inputs; C2: numerical inputs; C3, C4, C5: Japanese inputs). Of 15 pairwise axis comparisons under permutation testing with Benjamini–Hochberg correction, 14 are statistically significant; only the C1–C2 comparison is not (q = 0.693). These results demonstrate that the six geometrically defined axes of Paper 1 are functionally heterogeneous: they differ in overall response magnitude, in whether they exceed a random-direction control at all, in the direction of their sign asymmetry, and in which input category they are most sensitive to. The results do not establish a single, complete ranking of axis importance; in particular, C1 and C2 are not statistically distinguishable in pooled response magnitude, and the ordering of C4 and C5 relative to random directions depends on which control comparison is used.

title: Source code and data sets used in the experimental evaluation of the ALENEX 2027 Paper "Practical and Space-Efficient LZ77 and LZ Pre-Compression via String Synchronizing Sets"
abstract: This artifact accompanies the paper "Practical and Space-Efficient LZ77 and LZ Pre-Compression via String Synchronizing Sets" by Jonas Ellert and Lukas Nalbach. The paper presents practical and space-efficient algorithms for computing exact and approximate LZ77 factorizations using string synchronizing sets. The implementations include an optimized LZ77 3-approximation algorithm, an exact LZ77 factorization algorithm, and a variant of the exact algorithm employing sparse prefix- and suffix-array interval sampling. The artifact also includes ssszip, a parallel pre-compression tool based on the perfect phrases of the approximate LZ77 factorization. Contents This artifact provides the C++20 implementation of the presented algorithms and the accompanying experimental framework for reproducing the results reported in the paper. The implementation includes: An optimized algorithm for computing a 3-approximate LZ77 factorization. An exact LZ77 factorization algorithm, including a variant with sparse interval sampling. Parallel implementations of the factorization algorithms. The ssszip compression and decompression tool. Benchmark programs for evaluating factorization performance, compression throughput, compression ratio, and peak memory consumption. Experimental Datasets The experimental evaluation uses three highly repetitive benchmark texts, each with a size of 50 GB: sars2: A collection of SARS-CoV-2 genomes. chr19: A collection of concatenated human chromosome 19 haplotypes. dewiki: A highly repetitive text constructed from German Wikipedia entries. The genomic datasets were constructed from data obtained from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). The benchmark texts and the instructions for obtaining them are available through the GitHub repository linked below. Reproducibility The artifact supports the reproduction of the experimental evaluation presented in the paper, including the comparison of the proposed LZ77 factorization algorithms with existing approaches and the evaluation of ssszip against other compression tools. The experiments cover factorization throughput, approximation ratio, peak memory consumption, parallel scalability, compression ratio, and compression and decompression throughput. The accompanying repository provides build instructions, benchmark programs, and information on obtaining the experimental datasets. Source Code and Documentation The source code, benchmark programs, and documentation are available at: https://github.com/LukasNalbach/lz77-sss The full version of the ALENEX paper is available on arXiv.org: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30193 This Zenodo record provides an archived version of the software and accompanying experimental materials for the ALENEX 2027 Artifact Evaluation.

title: Noise-Robust Distributed PV Power Prediction with Sampling-Noise Awareness
abstract: This paper presents a forecasting strategy for distributed photovoltaic (PV) systems using the echo state network (ESN), aiming to improve forecasting performance with data noise at sampling points of dispersed PV data collection devices. In real-world scenarios, noisy and non-normally distributed data caused by sensor malfunctions, human errors, and extreme weather lead to outliers, thereby undermining the reliability of power generation forecasting algorithms. Therefore, we propose an outlier-robust echo state network (OR-ESN) that leverages the combined strengths of ridge regularization and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regularization to achieve enhanced generalizability and sparsity. Furthermore, by adopting the ℓ1-norm as the loss function, the model achieves robust performance in the presence of noise. In addition, as distributed PV systems are increasingly preferred because of their flexibility, efficiency, and economic advantages, we extend the OR-ESN to the distributed outlier-robust echo state network (DOR-ESN) to better meet the forecasting needs of distributed PV systems. Furthermore, the distributed average consensus protocol is introduced and combined with the ADMM algorithm to enhance communication efficiency during the training process of the distributed ESN network for power prediction. The experimental results show that the OR-ESN and DOR-ESN demonstrate excellent predictive performance. Specifically, the OR-ESN increases the resistance to perturbations due to noise in distributed PV power forecasting. Moreover, the DOR-ESN builds on this foundation to significantly improve the accuracy and adaptability of power predictions for distributed PV systems.

title: Two Heads Are Better Than One: A Multi-Task Learning Framework for Robustness Against Adversarial Text Perturbations
abstract: Sentiment analysis models deployed in real-world applications face significant threats from adversarial attacks that perturb the text input at the character and word levels. While adversarial robustness has been extensively studied in NLP, most approaches focus solely on improving robustness against a single attack type. This paper introduces a unified multi-task learning framework that jointly trains a DeBERTa-v3 encoder with two classification heads: (1) sentiment classification (primary task), and (2) attack-type detection (auxiliary task). Our key finding is counter-intuitive: jointly training on attack-type detection, despite being an ostensibly unrelated auxiliary task, measurably improves sentiment robustness against both attack types. We conduct a rigorous six-stage experimental study — spanning a pilot comparison of five loss-weighting strategies, a hyperparameter sweep, full-scale confirmatory training, a controlled ablation ladder, and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization testing. The primary model, trained with a fixed loss-weight ratio (λₐ = 0.3), achieves 83.28% overall sentiment accuracy on in-distribution test data, with 77.84% robustness on character-level attacks and 84.16% on word-level attacks. A single-task sentiment-only baseline trained under identical conditions reaches only 79.18%, demonstrating that auxiliary attack-type supervision acts as a robustness-improving regularizer. External evaluation on independently-generated TextAttack adversarial samples confirms generalization beyond the training pipeline, with 83.33% accuracy on character-attacked samples and 85.00% on word-attacked samples.

title: PreGS: A Parameter-Transfer-Based Multi-Expert Graph Neural Network for Node Classification
abstract: Graph neural networks have achieved strong performance in node classification by aggregating information from graph neighborhoods. However, a single aggregation mechanism may be insufficient to capture diverse structural patterns across graph datasets. Moreover, independently training multiple structural branches can introduce substantial overhead without necessarily producing stable node representations. To address these issues, this paper proposes PreGS, a parameter-transfer-based multi-expert graph neural network framework. PreGS first pretrains a multi-head graph attention network (GAT) and transfers the linear transformation weights of its first-layer attention heads to multiple GraphSAGE experts. The transferred experts are frozen and used as complementary structural branches. The fused raw node features, GAT head representations, and GraphSAGE expert representations are fed into a multilayer perceptron (MLP), whose output is further fused with the pretrained GAT logits. Based on PreGS, we further develop PreGSv2, which introduces source-level weighting and a structural gating mechanism for adaptive multi-source feature integration. Experiments on eight public graph datasets show that PreGS and PreGSv2 achieve competitive performance against representative graph neural network baselines. Ablation, parameter-transfer, sensitivity, aggregator, visualization, and training-time analyses further validate the effectiveness and stability of the proposed framework. The code and datasets are available at https://github.com/LH-Czc/PreGS.
